other_side: Where this edition treats reading a model's inner workspace as a lever to build better models, Zitron's standing argument is that the models are not, in any commercially meaningful way, getting better — and that the research pageantry around them is part of the con. He frames generative AI as a technology built "to ingratiate at the highest cost possible", sustained by "hype, deceit and mythology" rather than capability gains. His harder point is financial: he argues the sector needs "$3 trillion or more in revenue by end of 2030 to sustain its existence" against data-centre buildouts he estimates at $9.5 to $15 trillion, money he says the banks cannot issue. On that reading, an elegant interpretability breakthrough at Anthropic changes nothing about the arithmetic that decides whether any of this survives; it is a sharper window onto a system whose economics have already stalled.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether deeper understanding of a model's internals converts into capability worth the capital being spent. Both accept two facts: no one hand-programs these systems, so their inner logic is genuinely opaque, and the industry now rests on enormous, unrecouped spending. The empirical question that will resolve is whether interpretability-guided methods like counterfactual reflection training produce measurable, durable reliability gains in shipped models over the next year or two — the observable that settles it is real-task error rates on the next release cycle, not lab demos. The residue is pure worldview: a young science of machine minds versus manufactured consent dressed as research. NLW is vindicated if the technique reliably lifts performance in production; Zitron if capability keeps plateauing while costs climb. Both are polemicists with incentives — NLW bullish and anti-doom, Zitron bubble-certain and anti-hype — so the signal is where they quietly agree: this is early and uncertain, not magic. Watch the next model release for interpretability-attributable gains.
